pairs.title: Ladder and greenhouse
pairs.version_a: Ken borrowed a long wooden ladder from his neighbor Ruth without asking her, to clear leaves from his gutter. When he finished, he leaned the ladder against the side of Ruth's glass greenhouse and went inside for dinner, meaning to return it later. During the night a strong wind pushed the ladder against one glass panel, and the panel shattered. The panel had been in good condition. Without the ladder, it would have survived the wind. Ruth had to pay for a new panel the next morning.
pairs.version_b: Ken borrowed a long wooden ladder from his neighbor Ruth without asking her, to clear leaves from his gutter. When he finished, he leaned the ladder against the side of Ruth's glass greenhouse and went inside for dinner, meaning to return it later. During the night a strong wind pushed the ladder against one glass panel, and the panel shattered. The panel had been loose for weeks. Even without the ladder, it would have blown out in the wind. Ruth had to pay for a new panel the next morning.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether the panel would have survived the wind without the ladder (A) or would have blown out anyway (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was it of Ken to leave the ladder leaning against the greenhouse?
pairs.comprehension_question: Where did Ken leave the ladder?
pairs.option_a: Against the side of Ruth's greenhouse
pairs.option_b: Against the wall of his own house
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers tend to judge an action as worse when the harm depended on it, but the identical action and identical harm will limit the gap.
pairs.originality_note: An original everyday borrowed-ladder case, not a re-skin of a known preemption or trolley vignette.

pairs.title: Office circuit overload
pairs.version_a: A small office has a rule: nobody may plug a space heater into the shared power strip, because it can overload the circuit. Sam, who read this rule in the staff handbook, plugged his space heater into the strip on a cold morning. Later that morning Lee plugged an electric kettle into the same strip, which was allowed. Together the heater and the kettle drew too much power, the circuit breaker tripped, and the office computers shut off. Everyone lost the work they had not yet saved.
pairs.version_b: A small office has a rule: nobody may plug a space heater into the shared power strip, because it can overload the circuit. Sam, who was never told about this rule and never saw it in the staff handbook, plugged his space heater into the strip on a cold morning. Later that morning Lee plugged an electric kettle into the same strip, which was allowed. Together the heater and the kettle drew too much power, the circuit breaker tripped, and the office computers shut off. Everyone lost the work they had not yet saved.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether Sam knew about the rule against plugging in space heaters (A) or was never told about it (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How much did Sam cause the computers to shut off?
pairs.scale_label_1: Did not cause it at all
pairs.comprehension_question: What did Lee plug into the power strip?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Causal ratings are usually higher when the rule-breaker knew the rule, but Sam's action and Lee's contribution are identical, so the gap should be modest.
pairs.originality_note: An original office power-strip case with two contributors, not a copy of the published pen-taking or similar rule-violation vignettes.

pairs.title: Babysitter shop trip
pairs.version_a: Nina was babysitting a four-year-old boy who had fallen asleep upstairs. The parents were out for the evening. Nina realized she had forgotten to buy milk for his breakfast. She knew there was a small chance he might wake up and need her, but she decided to leave him alone and walk to the corner shop, ten minutes round trip. While she was gone, a loud clap of thunder rolled over the house. The boy slept through it, and Nina came back to find him still asleep. Nothing went wrong.
pairs.version_b: Nina was babysitting a four-year-old boy who had fallen asleep upstairs. The parents were out for the evening. Nina realized she had forgotten to buy milk for his breakfast. She knew there was a small chance he might wake up and need her, but she decided to leave him alone and walk to the corner shop, ten minutes round trip. While she was gone, a loud clap of thunder rolled over the house. The boy woke up, fell down the stairs, and broke his arm before Nina came back.
pairs.intended_difference: The boy sleeps through the thunder and is fine (A) or wakes up and breaks his arm in a fall (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Nina's choice to leave the boy alone and go to the shop?
pairs.comprehension_question: Why did Nina go to the corner shop?
pairs.option_a: To buy milk for the boy's breakfast
pairs.option_b: To pick up the boy's parents
pairs.option_c: To buy medicine for the boy
pairs.prediction_rationale: Many readers let a bad outcome color their view of the choice even when told the risk was the same, though instructed to judge the choice itself, so I expect a modest gap.
pairs.originality_note: An original babysitter-and-thunder case, not the drunk-driving or similar standard moral-luck examples.
